definitions.definition: The quantity of a good or service that consumers are willing and able to purchase at each possible price over a given period of time, ceteris paribus.
The quantity of a good or service that producers are willing and able to produce and sell at each possible price over a given period of time, ceteris paribus.
As the price of a good rises, the quantity demanded falls, ceteris paribus — there is an inverse relationship between price and quantity demanded.
The situation where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied, so there is no tendency for the price to change. The market clears at the equilibrium price.
A Latin phrase meaning 'all other things being equal' — the assumption that all other variables are held constant when analysing a relationship between two variables.
A measure of the responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in price, calculated as the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in price.
A measure of the responsiveness of demand to a change in consumer income, calculated as the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in income.
A measure of the responsiveness of quantity supplied to a change in price, calculated as the percentage change in quantity supplied divided by the percentage change in price.
A legal maximum price set by the government below the equilibrium price, intended to make a good more affordable. It results in excess demand (a shortage).
A legal minimum price set by the government above the equilibrium price, intended to support producers or workers. It results in excess supply (a surplus).
A tax imposed on spending on goods and services, paid to the government by the seller. It increases firms' costs of production, shifting the supply curve upwards by the amount of the tax.
A payment per unit of output made by the government to firms, lowering their costs of production and shifting the supply curve downwards by the amount of the subsidy.
A price floor in the labour market: the lowest wage that employers may legally pay workers, set above the equilibrium wage to raise the incomes of low-paid workers.
The failure of the free market to allocate resources efficiently, resulting in an over-allocation or under-allocation of resources relative to the social optimum.
A cost or benefit of production or consumption experienced by third parties, for which no compensation is paid. Externalities are not reflected in the market price.
A cost imposed on third parties by producers (e.g. pollution), so that marginal social cost exceeds marginal private cost (MSC > MPC) and the good is over-produced by the market.
A cost imposed on third parties by consumers (e.g. second-hand smoke), so that marginal social benefit is below marginal private benefit (MSB < MPB) and the good is over-consumed.
A benefit enjoyed by third parties from consumption (e.g. vaccination), so that marginal social benefit exceeds marginal private benefit (MSB > MPB) and the good is under-consumed.
A good that creates positive externalities of consumption and is under-provided and under-consumed by the free market (e.g. education, healthcare).
A good that creates negative externalities of consumption and is over-provided and over-consumed by the free market (e.g. cigarettes, sugary drinks).
A good that is non-excludable and non-rivalrous (e.g. street lighting). The free-rider problem means it will not be provided by the free market.
Resources that are rivalrous but non-excludable (e.g. fish stocks, clean air). They are vulnerable to overuse and depletion — the 'tragedy of the commons'.
A market structure with a single seller of a good with no close substitutes, protected by high barriers to entry, giving the firm significant market power over price.
A market structure dominated by a few large, interdependent firms, with high barriers to entry. Firms may compete or collude.
A theoretical market structure with very many small firms selling a homogeneous product, no barriers to entry, and perfect information — each firm is a price taker.
Profit above normal profit, earned when total revenue exceeds total economic costs (including opportunity costs).
The idea that consumers' ability to make rational choices is limited by imperfect information, limited time, and limited cognitive ability — so they 'satisfice' rather than maximise.

A behavioural-economics technique that alters people's behaviour in a predictable way by changing the choice architecture (e.g. default options), without forbidding options or changing prices significantly.
The total monetary value of all final goods and services produced within a country's borders in a given period of time, regardless of who owns the factors of production.
The total income earned by a country's residents and businesses, equal to GDP plus net income received from abroad.
GDP adjusted for changes in the price level (inflation), measuring the actual volume of output in constant prices so that different years can be compared meaningfully.
The total spending on domestic goods and services at each price level over a given time period: AD = C + I + G + (X − M).
The total quantity of goods and services that all firms in an economy are willing and able to produce at each price level over a given time period.
A situation where real GDP is below potential output because aggregate demand is insufficient, resulting in unemployment above the natural rate.
A situation where real GDP is above potential output because aggregate demand is excessive, putting upward pressure on the price level.
A sustained increase in the general (average) price level of goods and services in an economy over time, usually measured by the Consumer Price Index (CPI).
A sustained decrease in the general price level of goods and services in an economy over time (a negative inflation rate).
A fall in the rate of inflation — prices are still rising, but more slowly than before.
People of working age who are actively seeking work but are without a job. The unemployment rate is the number of unemployed as a percentage of the labour force.
An increase in real GDP over time; in the long run, an increase in the potential output of an economy (an outward shift of the LRAS or PPC).
A measure of income inequality derived from the Lorenz curve, ranging from 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (perfect inequality).
A situation where people lack the income needed to meet basic needs such as food, shelter and clothing — commonly measured against the international poverty line (US$2.15 per day, PPP).
The use of government spending and taxation to influence aggregate demand and the level of economic activity.
The use of interest rates and the money supply by the central bank to influence aggregate demand, typically to meet an inflation target.
The ratio showing that an initial injection into the circular flow leads to a larger final increase in real GDP: k = 1 / (1 − MPC) = 1 / MPW.
Government policies designed to increase the productive capacity (potential output) of the economy by improving the quantity or quality of factors of production, shifting LRAS to the right.
The ability of a country to produce a good at a lower opportunity cost than another country. It forms the theoretical basis for the gains from trade.
International trade that takes place without any government barriers or restrictions such as tariffs, quotas or subsidies.
A tax on imported goods, which raises the domestic price, protecting domestic producers but reducing consumer surplus and creating welfare (deadweight) losses.
A legal limit on the physical quantity of a good that may be imported over a given time period, restricting supply and raising the domestic price.
Government intervention in international trade using barriers such as tariffs, quotas, production subsidies and administrative obstacles to protect domestic industries from foreign competition.
The value (price) of one currency expressed in terms of another currency.
An exchange rate system where the value of the currency is determined purely by the market forces of demand for and supply of the currency, with no government intervention.
An exchange rate system where the value of the currency is pegged to another currency (or a basket) and maintained by central bank intervention.
A fall in the value of a currency in terms of another currency under a floating exchange rate system, caused by market forces.
A rise in the value of a currency in terms of another currency under a floating exchange rate system, caused by market forces.
A record of all financial transactions between the residents of a country and the rest of the world over a given period, consisting of the current account, capital account and financial account.
The section of the balance of payments recording the balance of trade in goods and services, plus net primary and secondary income flows.
A group of countries that have agreed to reduce or remove trade barriers between themselves (e.g. free trade areas, customs unions, common markets).
A common market whose members adopt a single currency and a common central bank with a single monetary policy (e.g. the Eurozone).
Development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.
A composite indicator of development measuring average achievement in three dimensions: a long and healthy life, education, and a decent standard of living (GNI per capita, PPP).
Investment by a firm in productive capacity in another country, involving a lasting interest and a degree of control (e.g. building a factory abroad).

diagrams.title: Market Equilibrium: Supply & Demand
diagrams.explanation: The diagram shows the interaction of supply (S) and demand (D) in a competitive market. The demand curve slopes downward, reflecting the law of demand: as price falls, quantity demanded rises. The supply curve slopes upward, reflecting the law of supply. The intersection of S and D establishes the equilibrium price (Pe) and equilibrium quantity (Qe) at point E. At Pe the market clears: there is no shortage and no surplus, and no tendency for price to change unless the curves shift.

diagrams.title: Price Ceiling (Maximum Price)
diagrams.explanation: The government sets a legal maximum price (P max) below the equilibrium price Pe to make the good more affordable. At P max, quantity demanded (Qd) exceeds quantity supplied (Qs), creating a shortage (excess demand) equal to Qd − Qs. Consequences include non-price rationing (queues, waiting lists), the emergence of parallel (black) markets, and a welfare loss because fewer units (Qs) are traded than at equilibrium.

diagrams.title: Price Floor (Minimum Price)
diagrams.explanation: The government sets a legal minimum price (P min) above the equilibrium price Pe to support producers' incomes or workers' wages. At P min, quantity supplied (Qs) exceeds quantity demanded (Qd), creating a surplus (excess supply) of Qs − Qd. The government may need to buy up the surplus, and resources are over-allocated to this market, creating allocative inefficiency.

diagrams.title: Indirect (Specific) Tax
diagrams.explanation: A specific tax raises firms' costs of production, shifting the supply curve vertically upwards from S1 to S1 + tax by the amount of the tax per unit. The equilibrium moves from E1 to E2: the price paid by consumers rises from P1 to P2, and the quantity traded falls from Q1 to Q2. The tax burden is shared between consumers and producers depending on the price elasticity of demand, and the government gains tax revenue equal to the tax per unit × Q2.

diagrams.title: Subsidy to Producers
diagrams.explanation: A per-unit subsidy lowers firms' costs of production, shifting the supply curve vertically downwards from S1 to S1 − subsidy. The equilibrium moves from E1 to E2: price falls from P1 to P2 and quantity rises from Q1 to Q2. Consumers pay less, producers receive more per unit (the price plus the subsidy), but there is a cost to the government budget and a potential over-allocation of resources to this market.

diagrams.title: Negative Externality of Production
diagrams.explanation: Production imposes external costs on third parties (e.g. pollution), so the marginal social cost (MSC) lies above the marginal private cost (MPC); the vertical distance is the external cost. The free market produces at Qm where MPC = MPB, but the social optimum is Qopt where MSC = MSB. The market over-produces (Qm > Qopt), creating the shaded welfare (deadweight) loss. Policy responses include Pigouvian taxes, tradable permits and regulation.

diagrams.title: Negative Externality of Consumption
diagrams.explanation: Consumption imposes external costs on third parties (e.g. smoking, sugary drinks), so the marginal social benefit (MSB) lies below the marginal private benefit (MPB). The market consumes at Qm where MPB = MPC, but the social optimum is Qopt where MSB = MSC. The good is over-consumed (Qm > Qopt), creating a welfare loss. Governments respond with indirect taxes, regulation, and awareness campaigns to shift MPB towards MSB.

diagrams.title: Positive Externality of Consumption
diagrams.explanation: Consumption creates external benefits for third parties (e.g. vaccination, education), so the marginal social benefit (MSB) lies above the marginal private benefit (MPB). The market consumes at Qm where MPB = MPC, below the social optimum Qopt where MSB = MSC. The good is under-consumed (Qm < Qopt), creating a welfare loss of potential benefits. Governments respond with subsidies, direct provision, and positive advertising.

diagrams.title: AD/AS Macroeconomic Equilibrium
diagrams.explanation: Short-run macroeconomic equilibrium occurs where aggregate demand (AD) intersects short-run aggregate supply (SRAS), determining the equilibrium price level (PLe) and level of real GDP (Ye). AD slopes downward (wealth, interest-rate and trade effects); SRAS slopes upward because higher prices with sticky resource costs raise profitability. Shifts of either curve change the price level and real output.

diagrams.title: Deflationary (Recessionary) Gap
diagrams.explanation: The economy is in short-run equilibrium at Ye, where AD = SRAS, but Ye lies below potential output Yp (shown by the vertical LRAS). The distance Yp − Ye is the deflationary gap: aggregate demand is too weak to employ all resources, so cyclical unemployment exists. Expansionary demand-side policies (fiscal or monetary) can shift AD to the right to close the gap.

diagrams.title: Inflationary Gap
diagrams.explanation: The economy is in short-run equilibrium at Ye, where AD = SRAS, but Ye lies above potential output Yp. The distance Ye − Yp is the inflationary gap: excessive aggregate demand pushes output beyond capacity, causing upward pressure on the price level (demand-pull inflation). Contractionary demand-side policies can shift AD to the left to close the gap.

diagrams.title: Economic Growth (LRAS Shift)
diagrams.explanation: Long-run economic growth is shown as a rightward shift of the LRAS curve from LRAS1 to LRAS2, increasing potential output from Yp1 to Yp2. This is caused by improvements in the quantity or quality of the factors of production — investment in capital, education and training, technological progress, or supply-side policies. It is equivalent to an outward shift of the production possibilities curve.

diagrams.title: Tariff on Imports
diagrams.explanation: Under free trade the country imports at the world price Pw, consuming Q4 while domestic firms supply Q1 (imports = Q4 − Q1). A tariff raises the domestic price to Pw + t: domestic production expands to Q2, consumption falls to Q3, and imports shrink to Q3 − Q2. Domestic producers gain and the government collects tariff revenue, but consumers lose more — creating two deadweight welfare-loss triangles from inefficient production and lost consumption.

diagrams.title: Floating Exchange Rate Determination
diagrams.explanation: In a floating system the exchange rate is set by demand for and supply of the currency. Demand for the pound (D£) comes from foreigners buying UK exports and assets; supply (S£) comes from UK residents buying imports and foreign assets. Equilibrium at E determines the exchange rate ERe. Changes in trade flows, relative interest rates, inflation or speculation shift the curves and move the exchange rate.

diagrams.title: Currency Depreciation
diagrams.explanation: A fall in demand for the currency (e.g. due to lower export demand, capital outflows or negative expectations) shifts D1£ left to D2£. The equilibrium moves from E1 to E2 and the exchange rate falls from ER1 to ER2 — a depreciation. Exports become more competitive abroad while imports become more expensive, which may improve the current account over time (Marshall-Lerner condition, J-curve at HL).

examples.title: Rent Control in Berlin
examples.description: Berlin introduced a rent freeze (Mietendeckel) in 2020, capping rents at 2019 levels for existing contracts. This is a classic example of a price ceiling designed to make housing affordable. The policy was struck down by Germany's constitutional court in 2021, but it illustrates both the intended effects (lower rents for sitting tenants) and the unintended consequences (reduced rental supply, queues for flats, and a shrinking construction pipeline) of maximum prices.
examples.data_context: Rent cap at 2019 levels | Ruled unconstitutional April 2021 | ~1.5M rental apartments affected

examples.title: UK Sugar Tax (Soft Drinks Industry Levy)
examples.description: The UK introduced a levy on sugary soft drinks in April 2018 to reduce sugar consumption and address the negative externalities of obesity. The tax is tiered by sugar content, so manufacturers reformulated products to avoid it — demonstrating how a corrective (Pigouvian) tax can change producer behaviour, not just raise prices. Average sugar content in taxed drink categories fell sharply.
examples.data_context: Introduced April 2018 | Tiered: 18p/24p per litre | ~46% average sugar reduction in affected drinks

examples.title: UK National Living Wage
examples.description: The UK's National Living Wage is a legal minimum wage — a price floor in the labour market — set above the free-market equilibrium wage for low-paid work. It raises incomes for millions of workers, but economic theory predicts potential excess supply of labour (unemployment) at the higher wage, an effect debated intensely in empirical studies.

examples.title: Uber Surge Pricing
examples.description: Uber's surge pricing is a real-time illustration of the price mechanism. When demand for rides spikes (rain, concerts, New Year's Eve), the algorithm raises prices. The higher price rations rides to those who value them most (signalling and rationing functions) and incentivises more drivers onto the road (incentive function), moving the market quickly back towards equilibrium.
examples.data_context: Multipliers of 2–3x at peak demand | prices update in real time by area

examples.title: Japan's Deflation & Abenomics
examples.description: Japan suffered nearly two decades of deflation and weak demand after its asset bubble burst in the early 1990s — the textbook example of a persistent deflationary gap. 'Abenomics' (from 2013) combined ultra-loose monetary policy (negative interest rates, massive quantitative easing), fiscal stimulus, and structural reforms to try to shift AD right and restore inflation to the 2% target.
examples.data_context: CPI averaged ≈0% 1995–2012 | BoJ policy rate −0.1% (2016) | QE purchases peaked ~¥80tn/year

examples.title: US Post-Pandemic Inflation & the Fed
examples.description: After the pandemic, a surge in aggregate demand (stimulus cheques, pent-up savings) collided with supply-chain constraints, pushing US inflation to a 40-year high — an inflationary gap. The Federal Reserve responded with the fastest interest-rate tightening cycle in decades, a contractionary monetary policy designed to shift AD left and bring inflation back towards the 2% target.
examples.data_context: CPI peaked at 9.1% (June 2022) | Fed funds rate raised from ~0% to 5.25–5.5% in 16 months

examples.title: China's Long-Run Growth Miracle
examples.description: China's decades of rapid growth since its 1978 reforms show long-run economic growth as an outward shift of LRAS: massive investment in physical capital and infrastructure, urbanisation moving labour into higher-productivity sectors, technology transfer through FDI, and education expansion all raised potential output year after year.
examples.data_context: ≈9% average annual real GDP growth 1980–2010 | ~800M people lifted out of extreme poverty (World Bank)

examples.title: US Steel & Aluminium Tariffs
examples.description: In 2018 the US imposed tariffs of 25% on steel and 10% on aluminium imports on national-security grounds. Domestic steel producers expanded output and prices rose — exactly as the tariff diagram predicts — but downstream manufacturers (cars, machinery) faced higher input costs, and studies found the cost per steel job saved was far above the wage, illustrating the deadweight losses of protection.
examples.data_context: 25% steel / 10% aluminium tariffs (2018) | US steel imports fell ~27% in the following year

examples.title: Brexit Referendum & the Pound
examples.description: The night of the June 2016 Brexit referendum, sterling suffered one of the sharpest falls of any major currency in modern history. Expectations of lower investment and growth reduced demand for the pound — shifting D£ left in the floating FX market — and the currency depreciated to multi-decade lows. Import prices rose, pushing up UK inflation over the following year.
examples.data_context: GBP/USD fell ~13% within weeks of the June 2016 vote | lowest level since 1985

structures.title: Part (a) — 10-mark question
steps: Define the key term(s) in the question precisely.
Draw a fully labelled diagram (axes, curves, equilibrium points, arrows for shifts).
Explain the economic theory step by step, explicitly referring to your diagram (P1→P2, Q1→Q2).
Link every paragraph back to the exact wording of the question.
No evaluation is needed in part (a) — accuracy and clarity score the marks.

structures.title: Part (b) — 15-mark question
steps: Define the key terms and set up the theory quickly.
Draw the relevant diagram(s) and explain the mechanism.
Apply a real-world example — this is required for the top markband.
Evaluate: consider stakeholders, short run vs long run, assumptions and limitations of the theory, and alternative policies (CLASPP).
Finish with a justified conclusion that answers the question directly.

structures.title: Data Response — question structure
steps: Definition questions (2 marks): one precise sentence, no padding.
Calculation questions: show every step of working and include units.
Diagram questions: draw, label fully, and explain using information from the text.
Short explanation questions: apply theory directly to the case in the text.
15-marker: combine the text's evidence + your own knowledge + a real-world comparison, then evaluate and conclude.

structures.title: Policy Paper (HL only)
steps: Read the data pack carefully and identify the economic problem(s) it shows.
Answer the quantitative parts: show full working for every calculation.
Explain the relevant theory and link it to the data provided.
Recommend ONE policy: justify it with the data, and explain why it beats the alternatives.
Acknowledge the limitations of your recommended policy — balanced judgement scores highly.

structures.title: Commentary structure (Portfolio)
steps: Three commentaries of up to 800 words each, on three different news articles.
Each commentary must use a different unit of the syllabus and a different key concept.
Structure: brief article context → definitions → fully labelled diagram → analysis of the diagram applied to the article → evaluation.
Evaluation should weigh stakeholders, short vs long run, and the assumptions behind the theory.
The article must be published no earlier than one year before you write the commentary.
